    #16446. Trust Is The New Battleground For Customer Engagement

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (948 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Trust Is The New Battleground For Customer Engagement

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • James Garvert is the EVP of Fraud & Communications Solutions for TransUnion.
    • ​Engaging with consumers has never been more essential, or more difficult.
    • It has been revealed that every interaction depends on trust, yet consumers are more hesitant than ever to engage.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    James Garvert is the EVP of Fraud & Communications Solutions for TransUnion.

    ​Engaging with consumers has never been more essential, or more difficult. Amid the meteoric rise of AI-enabled scams, call spoofing and social engineering attacks, the challenges organizations face when trying to reach consumers seem insurmountable.

    It has been revealed that every interaction depends on trust, yet consumers are more hesitant than ever to engage. Many of the traditional warning signs consumers were trained to recognize have disappeared—consumers are on edge.

    And with good reason: It’s a jungle out there.

    In our recent global study, “61% of business leaders ranked fraud among the risks with the greatest potential business impact, ahead of cybersecurity breaches, compliance, customer churn, operational cost and reputational risk. More concerning, 58% stated they’re very or extremely concerned fraud is evolving faster than their organizations’ abilities to detect and prevent it.”.

    Sources indicate that historically, organizations have viewed fraud and engaging with customers as separate disciplines. But today’s threat environment makes it clear they’re deeply interconnected. In many cases, the communication channel itself—whether a phone call, text message, email or mobile app interaction—provides the first indication that fraud may be occurring.

    According to recent reports, consumers don’t experience fraud, identity and communication challenges as separate concerns. To them, it’s one experience, one problem. It’s a trust problem that’s reshaping the customer journey. In fact, 69% of consumers say they would switch vendors for stronger security.

    Trust has become the foundation for both customer engagement and fraud prevention.

    According to recent reports, at our recent Fraud & Communications Summit in Chicago, keynote speaker Matt O’Neill, a former U.S. Secret Service Special Agent and recipient of Gold and Silver Awards for distinguished service, shared insights from years spent working undercover as a banker, broker, money launderer and other personas. In these roles, he led multinational investigations into crypto-laundering networks and dark web marketplaces.

    It has been revealed that according to O’Neill, fraudsters are winning because fraud has evolved into a highly organized industry. He explained that scam operations now function much like large multinational corporations. Scam compounds are similar to call centers, complete with organizational structures, performance quotas, shift schedules and human resources departments. Unfortunately, many of these compounds operate under sophisticated criminal networks and employ workers who have been trafficked.

    It has been revealed that at the same time, the barrier to entry into the fraud world has never been lower. AI enables fraudsters to create convincing scams at scale in virtually any language, including cloned voices, deepfake videos and personalized social engineering campaigns. And it’s cheap.​.

    It has been revealed that the consequences of eroding trust extend well beyond fraud losses. Organizations often experience:.

    • Reduced marketing effectiveness.

    Ironically, the industries and brands most trusted by consumers are frequently among the most targeted by fraudsters, with the highest fraud instances related to auto lending, bank-issued and retail credit cards and unsecured personal lending.

    Sources indicate that according to Edelman, trust now rivals price and quality as a primary factor influencing consumer decision-making. Research highlights that “77% of consumers cited confidence their personal data is secure as the most important feature when choosing whom to transact with online.”.

    Organizations can strengthen trust by approaching fraud prevention and customer communications as a unified strategy.

    Industry observers note that traditional fraud controls were designed for predictable attacks. Today’s fraudsters adapt quickly, vary their tactics and coordinate attacks across multiple channels and sessions. Identity verification remains notable, but it only confirms who someone claims to be. It doesn’t determine whether the current interaction should be trusted.

    Here’s where identity verification falls short:.

    • KYC (Know Your Customer) controls are often strongest at onboarding, not throughout the customer lifecycle.

    • Devices, behaviors and risk profiles change over time.

    • Credentials can be compromised after verification.

    • Synthetic identities can appear legitimate on paper.

    Recent findings suggest that the most notable fraud signal is often not a single event. Any single signal can be manipulated or generate false positives. It’s the story that unfolds throughout an interaction. It emerges through relationships among users, devices, accounts, entities and sessions.

    Sources indicate that as if it wasn’t hard enough, AI has turbocharged fraud. In addition, labeling identified threats as AI-driven remains a challenge. That’s because it’s difficult to build comprehensive strategies with new AI fraud models evolving so rapidly.

    According to recent reports, while fraud practitioners know when an account was taken over, there’s right now no label for how it was taken over and whether AI drove the attack. As a result, the AI-attributed training set doesn’t exist yet for tracking that fraud, and detection stays anchored to heuristics and analyst judgment.

    To be able to engage effectively with consumers and prevent fraud, organizations must adopt continuous authentication and layered risk strategies.

    • Develop a comprehensive strategy—don’t address fraud in silos across your organization.

    • Form strategic partnerships with your cyber teams.

    • Correlate identity, device, behavioral and contextual signals in real time.

    In a recent development, the process is straightforward: Collect. Correlate. Score. Decide.

    Every phone call, text message, email and digital transaction represents a trust moment. Customers want confidence the organization contacting them is legitimate and their information and transactions are protected. Simply asking consumers to “trust us” is no longer enough.

    Verified identity, authenticated communications and real-time risk intelligence are becoming the foundation of trust in a digital-first world.

    Sources indicate that the future isn’t reactive fraud mitigation. It’s proactive trust at the point of interaction, by orchestrating identity, risk and communications intelligence across every customer interaction.

    Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

    #16439. Now what? Colts should have traded Daniel Jones when they had the chance

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1180 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Yahoo ↗ Open Full Page

    Now what? Colts should have traded Daniel Jones when they had the chance

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yahoo

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here's the Daniel Jones timeline for the past eight months — and stick with us, because it's a wild ride.
    • The Colts signed Jones to the largest two-year contract in NFL history despite coming off Achilles surgery a few months earlier.
    • The Colts kept Jones as their starter, without any new competition, this season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here's the Daniel Jones timeline for the past eight months — and stick with us, because it's a wild ride.

    The Colts signed Jones to the largest two-year contract in NFL history despite coming off Achilles surgery a few months earlier.

    The Colts kept Jones as their starter, without any new competition, this season.

    The Colts continued to put Jones as QB1 while he struggled, throwing interceptions in 10 of his 11 starts.

    The Colts reportedly listened to trade offers for their starting QB prior to the Nov. 10 trade deadline before ultimately passing.

    The Colts started Jones in Thursday's blowout loss to the Texans.

    The Colts released Jones on Friday.

    Whew. Caught up? Good. Now consider: Cutting Jones will cost the team nearly $15 million in dead salary-cap money, plus another $35 million for next year.

    Recent findings suggest that friday's move was nothing short of a stunner, if only from a financial standpoint. From a football standpoint, the Colts couldn't justify keeping him as the starter? Cutting him now, knowing what a hit they'd take? It almost feels personal at this point.

    Recent findings suggest that colts head coach Shane Steichen clearly had enough of him Thursday night. The speculation on why Steichen hadn't gone to Anthony Richardson Sr. sooner was that the coach might have trusted Richardson even less.

    Steichen might also be in self-preservation mode, trying to hold together a ship that was partially stripped before the trade deadline and already in rough shape before that. But assuming Steichen didn't reach his breaking point during Thursday's game, why did the Colts wait to get rid of him?

    And not only for nothing. It actually cost the Colts money and flexibility to release him now. It doesn't get much uglier than that.

    Daniel Jones' run with the Colts ends after 24 starts in which Indianapolis went 11-13.

    There have been credible reports that multiple teams inquired about Jones' availability before the trade deadline, including the Ravens and Vikings. Others might also have checked in on him. The Colts held firm. The Ravens got Jacoby Brissett and the Vikings landed Kirk Cousins.

    This feels like a major missed opportunity. By releasing Jones, the Colts got nothing and made their situation worse. Even with the potential return of a Day 3 draft pick and a slightly better impact on their salary cap, the Colts passed.

    Recent findings suggest that it should be noted that the Vikings feel great about Cousins, and it's possible that their interest in Jones was more of a fallback option. The Ravens? Brissett's numbers over the past two seasons have been slightly better, so it's fair to say that they might have preferred the QB they ended up with.

    But any potential interest in Jones should have been met with a take-him-off-our-hands type of offer — the kind a team couldn't turn down. Someone is going to sign him here in the coming days, and given all the QB injuries around the league, it wouldn't be a stunner to see Jones start a game at some point this season.

    It has been revealed that the Colts were more than willing to part with other assets prior to the deadline, including DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson and Josh Downs. They listened to offers for Jones and Jonathan Taylor but ended up keeping both. Taylor had 11 carries for 21 yards and four catches for six yards on Thursday. Jones struggled and was cut. Little of this makes sense.

    When general manager Chris Ballard was fired midseason and replaced by interim GM Ed Dodds, it felt like an opportunity for Dodds to earn the full-time job by starting the process of replenishing the Colts' draft pool. They've done that, but they've also thrown away large chunks of meat still on the bone.

    Sources indicate that dodds was dealt a tough hand (one he helped put together, for what it's worth), but it's arguable he has played it poorly — unless Jones' release was mandated from on high. That's possible. If it's true, the Colts' situation is even uglier than it appears.

    In a recent development, since Andrew Luck's shocking retirement in August 2019, the Colts have started 12 different quarterbacks. Jones' 24 starts were the most from that group in that span, but it's highly likely some latest names are added to the list next season. This franchise is starting to become synonymous with QB instability, and after two decades of having Peyton Manning and Luck, that's a bitter pill to swallow.

    The remaining options on the roster this season are Richardson and Riley Leonard. The Colts don't appear to have great belief in either one. They declined the fifth-year option on Richardson's rookie deal, making him a free agent this spring, and have been reluctant to give him much of a shot prior to now. Leonard was last seen in last year's Week 18 start and hasn't played a snap in 2026.

    The assumption is that Richardson will play elsewhere next season. He certainly has a chance to rewrite his story in Indy as Jones' replacement, but whatever he does down the stretch will likely serve as an audition for his next stop. Leonard could be back in 2027, but it's unlikely he'd be anything higher than a backup to start next season.

    The Colts could have waited until the offseason and made Jones a post-June 1 cut, with far less of a salary-cap footprint. The question of whether to keep Jones is settled, but the problems are only starting.

    The Sauce Gardner trade cost them next year's first-round draft pick, and though the pre-deadline trades netted them some Day 2 and 3 ammunition over the next two years, it still makes acquiring a quarterback tougher come springtime.

    In a recent development, the Colts can still move into the bottom of Round 1 for a quarterback in next spring's draft. But will there be a viable starting candidate available in that range? What was thought to be a banner QB crop in the 2027 NFL Draft is turning into more of a grab-bag situation, depending on which underclassmen declare.

    Recent findings suggest that perhaps an unexpected veteran or two could hit the market. The veteran route feels more likely now, at least from an immediate-starter perspective. But will there be starting-quality options? That hope feels dubious now. Kyler Murray, Geno Smith and Deshaun Watson are the caliber of names that could be options. Do any of them elevate this team or give the Colts much more than a bridge option?

    According to recent reports, you can forget about trading for Lamar Jackson. The Colts don't have the assets to compete. That holds true for any other potential starting QB who could be available via trade.

    In a recent development, the pathways to salvation appear quite limited. The head coach appears to be on thin ice. The Colts sunk major money into Taylor and Alec Pierce this offseason but have little to show for it.

    In short, the whole situation is a hot mess.

    #16434. Tech Report: When To End A Technology Pilot: 19 Warning Signs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1288 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: When To End A Technology Pilot: 19 Warning Signs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Technology pilots give organizations an opportunity to test new solutions on a limited scale, evaluate their potential and identify challenges before committing to a broader rollout.
    • For tech leaders, the challenge is distinguishing between setbacks that can be addressed by adjusting a pilot’s scope or timeline and more fundamental issues that call its viability into question.
    • A pilot without success criteria is not a pilot.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Technology pilots give organizations an opportunity to test new solutions on a limited scale, evaluate their potential and identify challenges before committing to a broader rollout. But not every pilot warrants further investment, and knowing when to end one can be just as important as knowing when to expand it.

    For tech leaders, the challenge is distinguishing between setbacks that can be addressed by adjusting a pilot’s scope or timeline and more fundamental issues that call its viability into question. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council share warning signs that indicate it’s time to end a technology pilot rather than extend it, redesign it or move it into production.

    A pilot without success criteria is not a pilot. Defining boundaries and expectations, and, importantly, being transparent, are critical to a pilot’s success. Users should also share any uncertainty during the pilot instead of waiting for it to pivot or improve. - Arunava Sen, Tata Communications America Inc.

    A clear sign is when the pilot team cannot tell you what the technology accessed, what decisions it made, or what data it touched. If you cannot answer those questions in a controlled environment (test group), you will not answer them in production. - Michael Nicosia, Salt Security.

    Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

    One sign a technology pilot shouldn’t progress doesn’t involve the upcoming tech itself but the tools teams already work with. If teams are working in siloed workflows with tools that don’t collaborate with one another, introducing new technology can drive up costs, increase complexity and hurt productivity. Connected tools and workflows are integral to the success of any new tech deployment. - Usman Shuja, Bluebeam.

    According to recent reports, end a pilot when its success depends on hand-curated data that won’t exist in production. If someone cleaned the dataset, resolved definitions and fixed edge cases for the pilot, and no one owns doing that at scale in production, extending or redesigning the product in production won’t help. In many cases, technology isn’t the problem; the foundation is. Ask not whether the pilot worked, but what it worked on. - Prakash Reddy, Okta.

    If the pilot only works while its champion is in the room or while the vendor quietly does manual work behind the scenes, you’ve tested enthusiasm, not technology. Hand it to a team that didn’t build it for 30 days. If results collapse, you’d be pushing a dependency into production, not a tool. End it and keep the learnings. - Damian Wasserman, BEON.tech.

    When the team stops asking what we learned and starts asking when we get to stop, that’s the sign. A pilot without defined success criteria is avoidance. If you can’t name the specific business result it was supposed to prove or disprove, extending it won’t help. End it, define the outcome you actually need, and redesign around that from the start. - Ali Alkhafaji, APPLY.

    Organizations should end a technology pilot when they have full visibility of the tool’s usage and cost metrics but still cannot connect either to a meaningful business outcome. Adoption alone is not enough without a clear path to measurable value, and extending the pilot risks turning experimentation into ongoing spend without a business case. - Conal Gallagher, Flexera.

    A clear sign is when the people who were supposed to benefit stop asking about it. Pilots drag on because the sponsors like the idea, not because people need it. If the pilot group has quietly gone back to their old way of working and nobody complains when the tool goes down, there’s nothing to extend. Name the lesson, thank the team and end it. - Hastimal Jangid, Coozmoo Digital Solutions, Inc.

    According to recent reports, A pilot should be reconsidered when it performs well in a demo but can’t prove that it solves a real business problem. AI makes it easy to add capabilities, but more features don’t always mean more value. Teams need clear measures of success and feedback loops to understand what’s working and what’s not before investing further. - Tony Grout, M-Files.

    A clear sign to end a technology pilot is when it repeatedly fails to demonstrate measurable business value despite validated assumptions and reasonable adjustments. If the solution cannot deliver meaningful ROI, operational efficiency or strategic impact, extending it only increases sunk costs. Strong leadership means knowing when to stop, not just when to scale. - Kameshwar Singh, Cohesity.

    End a pilot if no effort was spent defining the vision and how value will be realized at scale. That’s like building a bridge from both ends without deciding where it should meet. - Venky Ramesh, LatentView Analytics.

    According to recent reports, A pilot should end when success depends on conditions that production will never have: handpicked data, expert owners, manual fixes, privileged integrations or constant vendor support. If removing that scaffolding collapses the value case, extending the pilot only perfects the illusion. The real test is not, “Does it work?” but, “Does it still create measurable value when exposed to ordinary users, messy data, real constraints and an ordinary day?” - Nicola Sfondrini, PWC.

    End a pilot when making the technology operable, reliable and governable outweighs its business value. If protecting sensitive data, maintaining an audit trail and providing human oversight would cost more than the expected benefit, extending that particular pilot needs a stronger business case than the time and money already invested. - Brian Stimpfl, S-Docs.

    Sources indicate that end a pilot when the evidence invalidates its core business premise. If customers can complete the workflow but gain no meaningful time, cost or quality improvement over the current process, more engineering won’t create demand. Define that minimum benefit before launch, test it with real users, and stop when it remains out of reach. - Irina Shymko, Langate Software.

    End the pilot when the team cannot define a credible path from the experiment to a measurable business outcome. If success still depends on vague future improvements, heroic manual support or assumptions the pilot was supposed to validate, extending it usually just delays the decision. - Dhyey Mavani, Abridge.

    It has been revealed that A pilot should end when the team cannot explain what latest evidence another extension will produce. Every extra week should answer a specific open question about value, risk, adoption, cost or scale. Once the remaining time is only keeping the pilot alive, the experiment has already delivered its answer. - Sibasis Padhi, Walmart Inc.

    I would end a pilot when it successfully completes individual tasks but repeatedly fails to deliver the full business outcome. Often, the underlying issue is the absence of a clear decision model for handling exceptions, approvals or unresolved work across teams. If nobody can authorize what happens next, scaling the technology only scales the problem. - Vamshi Noothi, Cisco.

    A pilot should be ended if nobody uses it unless someone reminds them. A pilot that only stays alive while its sponsor keeps pushing won’t survive production, and extending it just postpones that answer. Software nobody uses isn’t free; it still costs money to run, maintain and support. End it, write down what you learned about the problem, and put the team on something people actually want. - Jeremy Suriel, Kustomer.

    A clear sign to end a technology pilot is when no business owner is willing to take responsibility for implementation. Even if the technology performs well, success requires business ownership, accountability and commitment to change. Without a sponsor willing to champion the solution, allocate resources and own the outcomes, extending the pilot is unlikely to deliver value. Technology cannot create lasting benefits without clear business ownership. - Eranda Maldeniya, Enterprise Analytics.

    Brown, 29, injured his hamstring during Week 10's 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Munich. He got hurt in the fourth quarter and did not return, finishing with two catches (on six targets) for 27 yards.

    In his first season with the Patriots, Brown has already missed six of the team's 10 games. First, he sustained a high ankle sprain in the season opener and sat out four games while on injured reserve. Then he was sidelined for an additional two games due to a strained knee.

    The news on Brown comes as the Patriots also officially confirmed that quarterback Drake Maye suffered a fractured right fibula against the Lions and could miss the remainder of the regular season.

    Fresh England dropped to 5-5 following the defeat versus Detroit and has lost three of its past four games. The Patriots have a bye for Week 11, then visit the Los Angeles Chargers (1-8) in Week 12. New England is still in the AFC playoff race, just one game behind the Cleveland Browns (6-4) for the conference's third wild-card berth.

    In a recent development, with Brown injured, the Patriots' receiver depth chart consists of Mack Hollins, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism III and Kyle Williams. Romeo Doubs could join them after the bye week when he's eligible to be activated from IR. Douglas is the team's leading pass-catcher among wideouts with 32 receptions for 438 yards and four touchdowns.

    Industry observers note that brown was acquired from the Philadelphia Eagles during the offseason, trading a 2028 first-round pick and 2027 fifth-round selection. He registered 1,003 receiving yards last season with the Eagles (his lowest total in four seasons). However, Brown had reportedly become frustrated with quarterback Jalen Hurts — and his role in the Eagles' offense.

    Philadelphia traded Brown before a three-year, $96 million extension kicked in that takes him through the 2029 season.

    Brown is in his eighth NFL season, beginning his career with the Tennessee Titans. He was the team's second-round selection (No. 51 overall) out of Ole Miss and played with the team for three seasons.

    The 6-foot-1 receiver was dealt to the Eagles during the 2022 NFL Draft for first- and fourth-round picks. He subsequently received a four-year, $100 million extension from Philadelphia.

    A three-time Pro Bowler and two-time second-team All-Pro selection, Brown has 535 career receptions for 8,157 yards and 56 touchdowns.

    Take-Two Interactive vs. Anthropic: Which Market-Moving Stock Is the Better Buy?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Take-Two Interactive (TTWO +0.65%) and Anthropic (ANT -8.50%) are arguably the two stocks that generated the most excitement this week.
    • Anthropic rolled out its IPO this week, as its Claude artificial intelligence (AI) assistant has generated investor excitement and driven massive revenue growth.
    • Despite that anticipation and the likely boost to Take-Two stock, I believe Anthropic is the better buy, and here's why.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Will Healy – Nov 20, 2026 at 4:33PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Take-Two Interactive (TTWO +0.65%) and Anthropic (ANT -8.50%) are arguably the two stocks that generated the most excitement this week.

    Anthropic rolled out its IPO this week, as its Claude artificial intelligence (AI) assistant has generated investor excitement and driven massive revenue growth. That may have been overshadowed by gamers who have awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), possibly since Take-Two released GTA 5 in 2013.

    Despite that anticipation and the likely boost to Take-Two stock, I believe Anthropic is the better buy, and here's why.

    Admittedly, Take-Two might be a more obvious choice since the anticipation for GTA 6 likely predates Anthropic's 2021 founding.

    Recent findings suggest that with that waiting game now over, Take-Two subsidiary Rockstar Games revealed that it sold 32.5 million copies of the game on day one, generating $3.79 billion in revenue. That is huge considering that the company reported $3 billion in the first six months of fiscal 2027 (ended Sept. 30). That was game-changing, figuratively and literally, for Take-Two stock, which also reported an 8% year-over-year revenue decline during the same period.

    Furthermore, net losses have left it without a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. Still, according to analysts, this sales boost puts Take-Two on track for an estimated 27% yearly revenue gain in fiscal 2027 and a return to profitability. That recovery could make investors more willing to pay its 30 forward P/E ratio.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Sources indicate that unfortunately, game releases are one-off events, and such temporary sales bumps tend to run their course quickly. Consequently, analysts believe the entertainment stock's revenue growth will slow to 6% in fiscal 2028, making the release unlikely to change the company's long-term value proposition.

    In contrast, Anthropic's gains are on track to be more than one-time. Companies from nearly all sectors of the economy are scrambling to incorporate AI into their businesses. This has greatly benefited Claude, which has stood toe-to-toe with the competition from OpenAI's ChatGPT and Alphabet's (GOOGL -2.70%) (GOOG -2.59%) Google Gemini.

    Its financials confirm its fast-growing popularity. The $33 billion it generated in the first nine months of 2026 far exceeded the $2.5 billion it reported during the same period in 2025.

    Moreover, although it lost $104 billion during the first three quarters of 2026, $94 billion of that loss resulted from changes in the fair value of convertible notes. The operating losses were less than $1.3 billion of that total loss, suggesting it could turn an operating profit in the foreseeable future.

Reports of a Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) accounting investigation added to mounting concerns surrounding the company's regulatory exposure, while growing skepticism over elevated AI valuations continued to weigh on the broader semiconductor industry.

    Selling pressure was particularly severe across the semiconductor industry. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -13.25%) plunged 13.26% to $424.32, while Broadcom (AVGO -12.19%) fell 12.12% to $304.65. The widespread losses suggest investors are reassessing the valuations and near-term outlook for AI-related companies, even as demand for advanced computing infrastructure remains strong.

    Recent findings suggest that nvidia's latest sell-off highlights a growing disconnect between the firm's financial performance and investor expectations. Despite reporting exceptional quarterly revenue growth and raising its outlook, shares have continued to decline alongside the broader semiconductor industry. With fresh SEC scrutiny of Nvidia's accounting practices and tightening U.S. semiconductor export restrictions adding to uncertainty, investors are increasingly questioning whether the company's exceptional growth can justify its valuation amid deteriorating market conditions.

    Recent findings suggest that looking ahead, the central question is whether Nvidia can sustain its growth and profitability as major technology companies face increasing pressure to demonstrate returns on their AI investments. A slowdown in data center spending, tighter export restrictions, or additional regulatory developments could force analysts to reassess Nvidia's earnings projections for 2027.

    Sources indicate that for investors considering buying the dip, the distinction between a falling stock price and an improving investment opportunity is particularly key. Nvidia's long-term competitive advantages remain substantial, but its valuation must be weighed against greater regulatory uncertainty and the possibility of slower industry growth. Until there is greater clarity surrounding the reported SEC investigation and signs of stabilization across semiconductor stocks, investors should remain cautious about assuming the recent sell-off has created a definitive buying opportunity.

    If I Could Tell All S&P 500 Investors Just 1 Thing Right Now, It's This

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 10 stocks we like better than Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ›.
    • Sources indicate that at one point in 2025, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) fell 19% below its high.
    • Recent findings suggest that in 2020, the index dropped by nearly 35% during the COVID pandemic.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By David Dierking – Nov 20, 2026 at 4:45PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ›.

    Sources indicate that at one point in 2025, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) fell 19% below its high. It still finished the year up 16%.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2020, the index dropped by nearly 35% during the COVID pandemic. It also closed out the full calendar year with a gain of 16%.

    Sources indicate that in 2026, stocks are sliding again. Right now, the S&P 500 sits about 6% below its all-time high, but the Nasdaq-100 is down nearly 13%.

    In a recent development, I don't tell you this to suggest that U.S. stocks are poised for a rapid recovery like they experienced earlier this decade. It's to tell you that episodes like this are part of the experience when investing in stocks.

    Sources indicate that if you own the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -3.42%), here's the one thing I'd tell you right now. These declines are no doubt painful, but they're the price of admission when accumulating long-term wealth.

    Industry observers note that here's an interesting bit of stock market trivia. Since 1980, the average intra-year drop in the S&P 500 has been 14.2%. But despite this, the S&P 500 has produced a positive calendar-year return in 35 of those 46 years.

    Industry observers note that in other words, market corrections are a normal and regular occurrence for the S&P 500. But so are the recoveries from them. And the fact remains that stocks spend much more time rising than they do falling. The short-term losses are part of the path to long-term gains.

    One of the most underrated moves an investor can make is making no move at all.

    In a recent development, when stock prices are falling, many people rush to sell their stocks, fearing that more losses are on the way. They may say something like they're going to wait for things to get "better" before they get back in.

    There are a couple of things wrong with that thinking.

    First, selling stocks after they've fallen only locks in the loss. It doesn't erase it. Second, stock market rebounds are often well underway by the time investors feel that things have gotten "better.".

    Recent findings suggest that the sum total of these actions means that a lot of folks lock in the loss, miss out on the rebound, and end up damaging their long-term returns. If the S&P 500's long-term annualized return is around 10%, the average investor usually ends up getting less than that.

    That's why the one thing I like to tell investors is: Get used to the stock market's volatility. It's normal and it's a daily occurrence. Corrections of 10% or more are fairly frequent and should be expected from time to time. It's how you handle them that makes the difference. If you can buy and hold instead of giving in to the temptation to sell, you have a better chance of reaching your financial goals.
